plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 15.2.12
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example that evaluates the line integral of F = cos(x) i + sin(x) j along two different oriented curves. The figure contains two panels (a) and (b), each showing the same vector field F drawn over a green-shaded background with the note Vectors not to scale. Panel (a): the oriented curve C is a short vertical red line segment at x = -pi/2, directed downards from y = 2 to y = 1. Panel (b): the oriented curve C is a parabolic arc from (-1, 1) to (2, 4), directed first down, then upward and to the right. The figure shows the two distinct integration paths for parts (a) and (b) of the example, making visible how each curve's geometry and alignment relative to the field vectors determines the computed line integral. Note that the two parts of the image are differently scaled.

interactionPlan.concept: The line integral of a vector field along a curve accumulates the dot product of the field and the curve's tangent, depending entirely on how the path aligns with the field.
elements: x and y axes with tick marks and labels (x, y, -π/2, -1, 1, 2, 3, 4)
Pale green shaded background region
Vector field F = cos(x)i + sin(x)j depicted as black arrows on a uniform grid
Red oriented curve C with direction arrows along the path
Label 'C' next to the curve
Red dot endpoints for curve C
Moving point on curve C (controlled by the parameter slider)
Tangent vector to C and the local field vector drawn at the moving point
Text overlay showing the local dot product and the accumulated line integral value

interactions.label: Curve C Path
interactions.teaches: Different paths through the same vector field yield different line integral values based on their varying geometry.
Freely reshaping the integration path by moving its start and end points instantly changes how it traverses the field, updating the integral.

interactions.label: Position along curve (t)
interactions.teaches: At any specific point along the path, the contribution to the total integral is determined by the alignment between the local tangent and the field vector.

demo_steps.title: Path A: Constant alignment
demo_steps.narration: Along the vertical path at x = -π/2, the vector field points straight down. Because the path also points straight down, the field and tangent are perfectly aligned, yielding a steady positive contribution.

demo_steps.title: Path B: Varying alignment
demo_steps.narration: Switching to the parabolic path changes the relationship. As the curve sweeps from left to right, its tangent direction changes, passing through field vectors that point down, then right, then up-right.

demo_steps.title: Accumulating the integral
demo_steps.narration: Sweep the position slider to trace the curve. The dot product of the local field vector and the tangent vector determines the integral's value at each step: positive when aligned, zero when perpendicular, and negative when opposed.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A line integral simply adds up the local alignment (dot product) between the vector field and the path's direction at every point along the curve.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Combine the two textbook panels into a single interactive Cartesian coordinate system. Draw the vector field F = <cos(x), sin(x)> as uniform-length arrows (since vectors are 'not to scale') over a pale green background. The 'pathSelection' toggle switches the red curve C between the vertical segment from y=2 to y=1 at x=-π/2, and the parabolic arc from (-1,1) to (2,4). Allow the red endpoints to be draggable to dynamically reshape the curve. The slider should move a distinct point along the active curve, sprouting two visible vectors (tangent and field) from that point to visualize the dot product.
